solutions.check: grid rebuilt from the blog's light list (unique); every answer written into it with each crossing agreeing

clue.text: Workers' organisation's functioning in US city

parts.note: the TUC is the Trades Union Congress, Britain's federation of trade unions; with the 's it gives TUC'S
a machine that is functioning is switched on

explanation.surface: A trade union body is up and running somewhere in America.
explanation.walkthrough: The TUC (Trades Union Congress) is the UK's umbrella body for trade unions; 'TUC's on' means its business is going ahead.
explanation.definitionFit: Tucson is a large city in southern Arizona, in the United States.

clue.text: Parasites cling, first to last

indicators.note: first to last means the opening letter is shifted to the end

parts.note: to stick is to cling or adhere

explanation.surface: Parasites grip their hosts tightly from start to finish.
explanation.definitionFit: Ticks are small blood-sucking arachnids that live on animal hosts, a classic example of a parasite.

clue.text: Prisoner getting more stupid — one may get charged

parts.note: con is short for convict, a prisoner
dense means stupid, so denser is more stupid

explanation.surface: A dim inmate, who may well face a new criminal charge.
explanation.walkthrough: 'charged' suggests being accused of a crime, but here it is electrical charge.
explanation.definitionFit: A condenser is an old name for a capacitor, a component that stores electrical charge.

clue.text: Burden — that we must cope with?

definitions.meaning: a burden is a responsibility or duty laid on someone
something that is our responsibility is said to be ..., read as two words

explanation.surface: A heavy load we simply have to bear.
explanation.definitionFit: Onus means a duty or responsibility, the burden of proof for example, so it is a direct synonym.

clue.text: Carriage fetched, losing little time in the morning

indicators.note: losing tells us a piece is dropped from the word for fetched

parts.note: to fetch something is to have brought it
T is the standard abbreviation for time
a.m. marks hours in the morning

explanation.surface: Someone collects a carriage early in the day and has a few minutes to spare.
explanation.definitionFit: A brougham is a light four-wheeled horse-drawn coach with an enclosed body, a kind of carriage.

clue.text: Recover, be on the up in the course of events

indicators.note: in puts the reversed piece inside the word for the course of events

parts.note: a round is a series or course of events, as in a round of talks

indicators.note: in a down entry going up means the letters read from the bottom upwards, reversed

explanation.surface: Bouncing back: things are looking up as matters run their course.
explanation.definitionFit: To rebound is to recover after a setback, like a market bouncing back.

clue.text: International body's taken the initiative to get imprisoned journalist released

indicators.note: to get imprisoned means the next piece is shut inside the others

parts.note: the UN is the United Nations, an international body; the 's adds S
to have led is to have taken the initiative
hack is a slang word for a journalist

explanation.surface: The United Nations acts first to free a reporter held in jail.
explanation.definitionFit: Unshackled means freed from chains, so set free or released.

clue.text: House, ruined, evicting one despicable person

indicators.note: evicting means throwing out, so the word one is removed

parts.note: undone means ruined, as in 'I am undone'

explanation.surface: A wrecked house has its tenant thrown out by a nasty landlord.
explanation.definitionFit: A hound is an old word for a contemptible man, a cur or scoundrel.

clue.text: Romeo diet, specially for a heavenly body

indicators.note: specially suggests the letters are arranged in a special new way

explanation.surface: A romantic lead goes on a special diet to look like a star.
explanation.definitionFit: A meteoroid is a small rocky body travelling through space, an example of a heavenly body.

clue.text: Sinister howl goes round tower after beheading

indicators.note: goes round means the word for howl is wrapped around the next piece

parts.note: to howl is to cry

indicators.note: beheading means the first letter of the word for tower is cut off

parts.note: a keep is the main tower of a castle

explanation.surface: A spine-chilling wail encircles a castle tower after an execution.
explanation.definitionFit: Creepy means causing unease or fear, a close synonym of sinister.

clue.text: Defeat a swinger in game, we hear

indicators.note: we hear says the word is identified by how it is spoken rather than spelt

parts.note: in the British children's game of conkers, a horse chestnut on a string is swung at the opponent's

explanation.surface: Beat a playground opponent at a game played by swinging something.
explanation.walkthrough: Conkers is a British schoolyard game: each player swings a horse chestnut (a conker) on a string to smash the other's.
explanation.definitionFit: To conquer is to overcome or beat, a straight synonym of defeat used as a verb.

clue.text: Bishop is with cross, having consumed one wafer?

parts.note: B is the chess notation for bishop

indicators.note: having consumed means the word for cross swallows the next piece

parts.note: to cross a line is to cut it, in the sense of intersect
I is the Roman numeral one

explanation.surface: A cross bishop takes a communion wafer during a service.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Wafer' seems to be the communion host, but the question mark shows it is just an example of a thin crisp biscuit.
explanation.definitionFit: A wafer is a thin crisp sweet biscuit, so it is one example of the class, hence the question mark.

clue.text: Retreating country folk mostly killed

indicators.note: retreating means going backwards, so the letters are read in reverse order
mostly means the last letter of the word for country folk is cut off

parts.note: the Welsh are the people of the country Wales

explanation.surface: People from the countryside withdrew, most of them having been killed.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Country folk' looks like rural people, but it means a nation: WELSH. 'Mostly' cuts it to WELS, and 'Retreating' reverses that.
explanation.definitionFit: Slew is the past tense of slay, so it means killed in the past-tense verb sense.

clue.text: A pet dog gun disturbed in drive

indicators.note: disturbed suggests the letters are thrown into disorder and rearranged

explanation.surface: A pet dog bothered by a gunshot in a driveway.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Drive' looks like a road at the end of the scene, but it is the noun meaning energy.
explanation.definitionFit: Get-up-and-go is an idiom for energy and enthusiasm, which is drive in the sense of motivation.

clue.text: Interrupting someone at match, American has disregard

indicators.note: interrupting means these pieces break into the middle of the word for someone at a match

parts.note: a match is also a marriage, at which the bride is a central figure

explanation.surface: An American cuts in on someone at a sports fixture, ignoring them.
explanation.walkthrough: 'match' suggests sport, but it means a marriage, so the someone is the BRIDE.
explanation.definitionFit: To brush aside is to dismiss or ignore, the same as to disregard.

clue.text: Ruined southern city once involved in exploit

indicators.note: involved in means these pieces are placed inside the word for exploit

parts.note: an exploit is a heroic deed
Troy was an ancient city, the setting of the Trojan War

explanation.surface: An ancient southern city brought to ruin by some daring act.
explanation.definitionFit: Destroyed and ruined are synonyms, both past participles meaning wrecked beyond repair.

clue.text: To cut out red meat may feature in my recommendations

definitions.text: meat may feature in my recommendations

parts.note: to die is to stop working, as an engine dies or cuts out
Titian is a reddish-brown colour, named after the Venetian painter

explanation.surface: A nutritionist advises dropping red meat.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface reads as a diet tip, but 'cut out' and 'red' are the wordplay; the definition is the rest, said by the expert.
explanation.definitionFit: A nutrition expert's advice could well include meat, so the phrase describes such a specialist in their own voice.

clue.text: Plateau with a black bird: the last to travel west

indicators.note: in an across entry west is leftwards, so the final letter moves to the front

parts.note: a rook is a black bird of the crow family

explanation.surface: A dark bird crossing an upland, the last of its flock heading west.
explanation.walkthrough: 'The last to travel west' takes the K at the end of AROOK to the front.
explanation.definitionFit: The Karoo is a vast semi-desert tableland in South Africa, a geographical example of a high flat region.

clue.text: War heroes dancing in carnival

indicators.note: dancing means the letters move about into a new order

explanation.surface: Returning war heroes dance at a street carnival.
explanation.definitionFit: A raree-show was a travelling peepshow or street spectacle, so a carnival entertainment.

clue.text: Thus street in Paris set about making money there

indicators.note: set about means turned round, so the letters are written backwards

parts.note: so means thus, as in 'so it was'
rue is French for street

explanation.surface: A Paris street sets about earning cash.
explanation.walkthrough: 'there' points back to Paris: the currency used in France.
explanation.definitionFit: France uses the euro, so euros are the currency, the money, of that country.

clue.text: Plant in ancient river protected by deity

indicators.note: protected by means these pieces are held inside the word for deity

parts.note: a deity is a god
olden means of former times, ancient

explanation.surface: A plant growing by an old river is guarded by a god.
explanation.definitionFit: Goldenrod is a tall perennial with yellow flower spikes, a garden and wild plant.

clue.text: Female relation, Peg, one receiving a sum of money?

definitions.text: one receiving a sum of money?

parts.note: gran is short for grandmother
a tee is the peg a golfer sets the ball on

explanation.surface: Granny Peg comes into some cash.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Peg' looks like a woman's name, but it is a golf tee.
explanation.definitionFit: A grantee is a person who receives a grant, a sum awarded for a purpose.

clue.text: Controversial book — not all allow it to be distributed

indicators.note: to be distributed means spread out and rearranged
not all means the word is incomplete, losing its last letter

explanation.surface: A notorious novel, not everyone being willing to let it circulate.
explanation.walkthrough: 'not all' cuts ALLOW to ALLO; with IT, those letters are rearranged.
explanation.definitionFit: Nabokov's novel about an older man's obsession with a girl was banned in several countries, a famously contentious book.

clue.text: Intransigent troublemaker left a message

parts.note: an imp is a mischievous troublemaker
a cable is a telegram, a message

explanation.surface: An unbending troublemaker departed, leaving a note behind.
explanation.walkthrough: 'left' looks like the past tense of leave, but it is L for left.
explanation.definitionFit: Implacable describes someone who cannot be appeased, a near synonym of intransigent and uncompromising.

clue.text: First piece in concert conveying energy

indicators.note: conveying means carrying, so the word for concert holds the next piece

parts.note: a prom is a promenade concert, as at the BBC Proms
E is the physics symbol for energy

explanation.surface: The opening number at a concert is full of energy.
explanation.walkthrough: The Proms are a long-running BBC summer concert series in London.
explanation.definitionFit: A proem is a preface or introduction to a book or speech, the opening section of a work.

clue.text: Churlish type exposed in speech

indicators.note: in speech says the word is identified by its spoken form

parts.note: bare means uncovered, exposed

explanation.surface: A rude person shows themselves up when they speak.
explanation.definitionFit: A bear is slang for a rough, ill-mannered, grumpy person, hence churlish type.

clue.text: Robber, not a Dick Turpin type?

indicators.note: not means the following letter is left out of the word for robber

parts.note: a raider is someone who attacks to rob

explanation.surface: A thief who isn't quite the famous highwayman sort.
explanation.walkthrough: Dick Turpin was an 18th-century English highwayman who robbed travellers on horseback.
explanation.definitionFit: Turpin rode the roads on his horse Black Bess, so he is one example of a horseman.

clue.text: First character in London street turned over barrier

indicators.note: first character in points to the opening letter of the street name
turned over means flipped upside down, and an inverted M looks like W

parts.note: The Mall is the road leading up to Buckingham Palace in London

explanation.surface: A barricade topples in a London street.
explanation.walkthrough: The Mall is the ceremonial road to Buckingham Palace. Turn its M upside down and it becomes W.
explanation.definitionFit: A wall is a solid structure that divides or encloses, a basic kind of barrier.

clue.text: Humorous type offering funny renditions, no end

indicators.note: funny suggests something odd, so the remaining letters are rearranged
no means the word end is removed from renditions

explanation.surface: A comedian performing amusing versions that never stop.
explanation.walkthrough: 'no end' looks like 'endlessly', but removes the letters END from RENDITIONS, leaving RITIONS, which 'funny' rearranges.
explanation.definitionFit: An ironist is someone who uses irony, saying the opposite of what they mean for humorous effect.

clue.text: Retro stuff at the Tate the woman had criticised

indicators.note: retro means backwards, so the letters are read in reverse order

parts.note: the Tate is a group of British galleries, so what it holds is art
she is the pronoun for a woman
'd is the contracted form of had, as in she'd

explanation.surface: A critic slates some retro exhibition at a London gallery.
explanation.walkthrough: The Tate is a group of British art galleries, Tate Modern among them. 'Retro' looks like a style, but it reverses ART.
explanation.definitionFit: Trashed is informal for harshly criticised, as in a reviewer savaging a show.

clue.text: Came to before the start of day, dazed before that

parts.note: numb means stunned, dazed
ere is an old word for before

indicators.note: the start of picks the opening letter of the word that follows

explanation.surface: Someone woke up before dawn, having been stunned before that.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Came to' looks like waking up, but it means totalled; 'before that' just sets NUMB at the front.
explanation.definitionFit: To number is to amount to, so a count that came to ten numbered ten.

clue.text: Fan club ultimately let down?

indicators.note: ultimately means in the end, so the final letter of club is taken

parts.note: to lower something is to let it down

explanation.surface: A supporter whose club has disappointed them.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Fan' looks like a supporter, but it is a machine that blows air.
explanation.definitionFit: A blower is a device that pushes air, an electric fan or heater for example.
